metadata.title: Windward
metadata.description: What the GB wind forecast said before each day-ahead auction closed, how far to trust it, and how much demand was left for other sources.

methodology.title: How it works
methodology.intro: Every number in Windward comes from data Elexon publishes. These are the steps that turn it into the figures on the other pages, and the limits to keep in mind.
methodology.stepsTitle: From raw data to the figures

sources.title: Collect what Elexon published
body: Wind forecasts come from WINDFOR. Forecasts are published about eight times a day, each looking up to two days ahead, and every one is kept with the time it was published.
Actual wind comes from FUELHH: metered output of wind farms connected to the transmission network, for every half-hour.
Demand forecasts come from NDF, the national demand forecast, which is updated roughly every half-hour. Actual demand comes from INDO. Both use the same definition of national demand.
Rows that are duplicated, negative or published after the hour they describe are dropped, and gaps are counted rather than filled.

alignment.title: Line up the hours
body: Wind forecasts are hourly, but actuals and demand data are half-hourly. Each hour's value is the average of its two half-hours, which matches the hourly blocks bought in the auction.

If either half-hour is missing, the whole hour is left out instead of guessed. Using only the half-hour that starts on the hour would change the January typical miss by about 18 MW, under 1%, so this choice doesn't drive the results.

selection.title: Pick the forecast a buyer actually had
body: Day-ahead power is bought in auctions that close the morning before delivery. For every delivery hour, Windward takes the newest forecast published before the chosen market's deadline, not a later one that buyers couldn't have seen.
New forecasts can land between two markets' deadlines, so buyers on different markets sometimes had different forecasts. The day-ahead page shows which forecast each market had.
If the newest forecast didn't cover an hour, the next newest one that did is used, and the hour is marked.

errors.title: Measure the misses
body: For each hour, the miss is the forecast minus what actually arrived. A positive miss means the forecast was too high, so a buyer who planned on it bought too little and had to make up the shortfall at balancing prices.
The typical miss is the average size of those gaps, ignoring direction. The average error keeps the direction, so it shows whether the forecast leaned high or low.

band.title: Work out a safer figure
body: Wind misses are bigger when the forecast is high, so hours are sorted into three groups by forecast level. Within each group, Windward looks at how actual wind differed from the forecast on every other pilot day.

The likely range runs from the 10th to the 90th percentile of those differences, with a small-sample correction so a short history doesn't make the range look tighter than it is. The bottom of the range is the safer figure: actual wind should beat it in about nine hours out of ten.
The day being shown is always left out of its own range, so the check isn't rigged. The day-ahead page reports how often the safer figure actually held across the pilot.
Wind that may not arrive is the forecast minus the safer figure, added up over the day.

demand.title: Add demand
body: The demand forecast is picked the same way as the wind forecast: the newest one published before the deadline, for each half-hour, averaged into hours.

Demand minus wind is what other sources such as gas, nuclear and imports must cover. Windward shows it twice: using the wind forecast, and using the safer figure, which is the amount to cover if wind comes in low.
This is national demand, not any one supplier's customers. Windward doesn't recommend a purchase volume. A supplier's own demand forecast could replace the national figure to make one.

caveats.title: Limits to keep in mind
body: The pilot covers one winter month. Its errors reflect that month's weather and may not hold in other seasons.
The data covers wind farms on the transmission network. Smaller wind farms on local networks show up as lower demand instead.
The likely range only reflects wind uncertainty. Demand forecast misses are reported separately and are not added to it.
The forecast ran high for most of January. One possible cause is wind farms being paid to turn down when the grid is congested, but that hasn't been checked here.
